newsitem.title: USA: Clinton defines centrist second-term agenda.
newsitem.headline: Clinton defines centrist second-term agenda.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, who hurt himself at the start of his first term by veering to the left of the political mainstream, vowed on Wednesday to lead from the "vital and dynamic center" over the next four years.

Defining his second-term agenda in his first major policy speech since Nov. 5, when he became the first Democrat since Franklin Roosevelt to win re-election, Clinton said his first priority was to balance the federal budget.

Clinton, who addressed the Democratic Leadership Council, a group devoted to promoting moderate policies, said he also intended to work to implement a tough new welfare reform law, push for campaign finance reform and improve U.S. education.
He said the American people, who left the Republicans in control of Congress in the election, had made it abundantly clear that they preferred pragmatism to polarisation.

"Today, the clamour of political conflict has subsided, a new landscape is taking shape. The answer is clear: the centre can hold, the centre has held and the American people are demanding that it continue to do so," he said.
"To make this democracy work, we must create a vital and dynamic centre that is a place of action. We cannot waste the precious gift of this moment."

It was a far cry from the president who departed from his campaign image as a moderate "New Democrat" upon entering the White House in 1993 by advocating liberal social reforms like allowing gays in the military and providing cradle-to-grave health care benefits for all Americans.

Clinton, who recast himself as a centrist after his Democratic Party suffered a political meltdown in the 1994 congressional elections, blurred distinctions between himself and the Republicans on an issue that not so long ago defined their differences -- how to balance the budget.

"Both parties now agree that we must balance the budget and both parties now agree that we can only do it in a way that reflects our deepest values and garners support from members of both parties," he said.

Implicitly acknowledging that critics of Democratic Party fundraising tactics in the 1996 election reflected widespread public dismay with the way the political system operates, Clinton also committed himself to campaign finance reform.

"Anyone who has been part of this system must in a moment of candor accept some responsibility for this and agree that it needs to change," he said. "There simply is too much money in our politics, it takes too much time to raise and inevitably it raises too many questions."
As Clinton spelled out his second-term goals, two of his most loyal liberal constituencies -- organised labour and black Americans -- were pushing rival candidates for the post of labour secretary.
The vacancy, created by Robert Reich's decision to return to private life, is among a half dozen top economic policy jobs that Clinton must fill in the near future.

Organised labour, with a powerful assist from Sen. Edward Kennedy, was pressing Clinton to nominate former Pennsylvania Sen. Harris Wofford to head the Labour Department. Blacks have rallied behind presidential assistant Alexis Herman.
White House and congressional sources said the backstage squabble seemed likely to be resolved by Friday, when Clinton plans a full-scale news conference.
They said he might also name replacements for Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor, Transportation Secretary Federico Pena amd National Economic Council director Laura Tyson.

The sources said New Mexico Representative Bill Richardson, who met Clinton on Tuesday night, was a strong contender for Commerce and that William Daley, the brother of Chicago Mayor Richard Daley, appeared to have the inside track for Transportation.
U.S. officials suggested leadership of the National Economic Council may be split between Gene Sperling, its current deputy, and Daniel Tarullo, the White House point man on global economic issues.
